cues.text: A Marriage in Trouble
In 1273, a newlywed woman of Lanciano named Ricciarella Stasio, desperate to restore the affection of her husband, Giacomo, consulted a woman locally reputed for sorcery.
The remedy she was given called for sacrilege: receive Holy Communion, carry the Host home unconsumed, burn it to ash over the fire, and slip the ashes into her husband's food or drink.
Flesh Instead of Ash
Ricciarella carried out the first steps, placing the Host in an earthenware jar set over the fire — but instead of burning to powder, the Host was transformed into living flesh.
Horrified, she wrapped the jar and its bloodied contents in a linen cloth and buried it beneath the manure of her husband's own stable, telling no one what she had done.
A Donkey That Would Not Pass
Strange events followed: every time Giacomo's donkey entered the stable, it stopped and knelt toward the very spot where the relic lay hidden.
The behavior was so consistent that Giacomo began to suspect his own wife had cast a spell on the animal, unaware of the far stranger truth buried beneath his own floor.
A Confession Seven Years Later
Only after seven years did Ricciarella confess her sacrilege to Giacomo Diotallevi , prior of the Augustinian priory in Lanciano and, as it happened, a native of the town of Offida .
He accompanied her to the stable, dug through the accumulated manure, and recovered the linen bundle, finding the flesh and the Host inside remarkably unspoiled.
Rather than leave the relic in Lanciano, he carried it back with him to Offida.
He later traveled to Venice to have a fitting reliquary made.
Historians have long read the removal as motivated at least partly by Offida's own interest in the prestige a Eucharistic miracle would bring the town.
Legacy

The relic remains today near the Church of St. Augustine in Offida, backed by a lengthy paper trail of confirming documents stretching from a decree of Pope Boniface VIII in 1295 to one of Sixtus V in 1585.
Ricciarella's own house in Lanciano was later transformed into a small chapel.
Offida still keeps the anniversary of the miracle each year on May 3.
The two towns' shared, centuries-long devotion to the same small relic has long outlasted whatever rivalry once separated them.
